choices.text: The student is right - only strong acids count as acids
Vinegar is a weak acid: it only partly releases its hydrogen ions, but it is still acidic
Vinegar is neutral because it is used in food

questions.feedback: If you agreed with the student, that is the trap: All acids are strong acids. Reteach point: Weak acids only partly release their hydrogen ions: vinegar is still acidic, just not strong. Strength is about how fully the ions are released, not about danger.
questions.prompt: A student says vinegar is not a real acid because real acids are all strong and dangerous. What is the best correction?

questions.answer: Red litmus turns blue in an alkali. Blue litmus turns red in an acid.
questions.feedback: A strong answer gives both changes the right way round: blue paper reddens in acid, red paper blues in alkali. If a paper does not change, the solution is neutral for that test.
questions.prompt: State the colour change when red litmus paper is dipped into an alkali, and when blue litmus paper is dipped into an acid.

questions.feedback: The salt takes its name from the acid: nitric acid gives a nitrate. Hydrochloric acid would give a chloride and sulfuric acid a sulfate.
questions.prompt: Nitric acid is neutralised by an alkali. What is the salt called?

questions.answer: The H+ ions from the acid pair up with the OH- ions from the alkali to form water. The leftover ions stay in solution and form a salt.
questions.feedback: A strong answer pairs the two ions into water first, then accounts for the leftovers as the salt. An answer saying the acid and alkali cancel into nothing has lost the salt.
questions.prompt: In one or two sentences, explain what happens to the H+ and OH- ions during neutralisation.
